Title: A new era of software engineering
Presenter: Walden Yan (Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer, Cognition)

spoken_segments.text: Hello, everyone. It's a pleasure to be here today. Quick introduction. I'm Walden. I'm one of the co-founders and chief product officer at Cognition. We build a AI product called Devin.
I want to spend most of my time here today though kind of abstracting a bit away from that and focusing on what are we doing internally as an engineering team to move way faster.

scenes.alignment_note: The speaker introduces himself and Cognition while standing in front of the opening title slide.

scenes.visual_summary: Bar chart illustrating a 40.4x increase in merged pull request (PR) volume at Cognition over a 12-month period (Oct 2025 - Oct 2026), compared against a 2.7x growth in engineering headcount (R&D) over the same period.
scenes.structured_reconstruction:
| Metric | Oct 2025 | Oct 2026 | Growth Factor |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Merged PR Volume | 1x | 40.4x | 40.4x |
| Engineering Headcount (R&D) | 1x | 2.7x | 2.7x |

spoken_segments.text: And so the backdrop I would put for all this is this is what our merged PR throughput looks like at Cognition. The start of this is around 12 months ago, so you're looking at about a snapshot of a year.
And over this last year, this blue chart here, this 40X is a 40X in the number of merged PRs we're producing on our engineering team.
Now you might also notice there's a small black line along the bottom there, it's easy to miss. But that 2.7X, that is our engineering headcount growth in the same period.

So we have been hiring engineers, but each of our engineers is now more than 10X more productive than they were before. And I would dare to say that these PRs are just as high quality, if not higher quality than they were a year ago.
And so really the crux of what I want to talk about today is what did we do to unlock this 40X engineering throughput?

scenes.alignment_note: The speaker points directly to the blue bar chart labeled '40.4x' for PR throughput and the dashed line at the bottom labeled '2.7x' for engineering headcount growth.

scenes.visual_summary: Section transition slide with the bold text statement 'We've transformed how we build' on a light patterned Cognition background.
scenes.structured_reconstruction: Section Slide: We've transformed how we build

spoken_segments.text: And there's a lot of things we did from both the code base to the way we structure engineering teams that I think are very practical steps you can take if you want to reproduce the same results.

scenes.alignment_note: Transition slide signaling the pivot to organizational and architectural changes implemented at Cognition.

spoken_segments.text: Many of you are probably familiar with the software factory. How many of you guys have heard of software factory? Let's see a raise of hands. Cool, so I'll start with the basics and then I'll work my way up to the more advanced stuff.

The basic idea of a software factory is, yeah, by default, everything should be self driving, um we have PRs that go from initial bug report to final merge and monitoring and maintenance without a single human involved.
oftentimes human judgment is needed though and that's where we have escalations. But by default our entire software development process is just run by Devon from end to end.

scenes.alignment_note: The speaker points to the horizontal stage sequence (Triage to Oncall) and highlights how Devin automates each step with human escalation fallback.

spoken_segments.text: One of the things this means is that the role of the software engineer has to change quite a bit. Around March of this year, we had this conversation with engineering team.

And we said, look, if you are right now just picking off tickets off a linear board and then setting that to an agent and implementing it, you're not going to really be set up for success in the age of AI.
because anything that is described and can be implemented, we'll be able to send to Devon. So really everyone has to change the way that they're developing.

And the way we've enforced this is we've taken our larger teams and we've broken them up into smaller pods. And these smaller pods not only are given swarms of agents to do work for them, they are given more vertical responsibility.

So instead you might have only two or three engineers on a team at a time, but they're responsible for everything beyond the engineering as well. They're responsible for listening to customer bug reports. They're responsible for doing QA testing. They're responsible for doing the PMing and product management and basically every engineer manages their entire own linear board of things to do.
And they send that to an agent to implement for them. So it's really a fundamental change in the way that our engineers do work.

scenes.alignment_note: The speaker contrasts the left-side role siloing with the right-side vertical pods containing 2-3 engineers deploying agent swarms.

spoken_segments.text: Another thing I'd really like to highlight is we work from Slack everywhere. So this is an example of what a customer bug report might look like. They send me a video on Slack.
And we just forward bug reports straight into our internal channel. And we tag Devin and say, hey, please fix this.
Devin immediately comes up, shows up at PR. But then also sends back a video with the fix and proof.
And this makes our lives so much easier because I I literally don't have to leave Slack for most of my work.

We've abstracted away all of the development to be based on evidence, videos, and I can just send the proof that the fix is ready right back to the customer without having to open an IDE or even GitHub most of the time.
So this is kind of the end goal you want to reach which is a point where you can do your entire development life cycle without opening up an IDE or without opening up a single coding agent.

Testing skills Devins fix and maintain them

spoken_segments.text: But to get to this point, there's a lot of infrastructure we had to change underneath. And so this is the hard part that really every engineering team has to do if they want to get to that point. It's not just you purchase a coding agent, you got to go change the way you build.

So before, when we tested our applications, we be testing them against cloud deployments. We'd have a staging environment, connect to a staging database, connect to live servers. And then we'd have our engineers manually go click through and verify that the flows work end to end.

We did a big migration to move every service to be able to run locally with Docker compose. We've made it so every third party service, we have mocked versions to be able to run locally. And these can all run inside a single virtual machine that every Devon has access to.

And every code agent in our company now does not need to touch any live services at all to test their changes. They, in fact, these VMs, we rebuild them every hour at the company. Every hour we pull the latest version of the code, we rebuild the entire codebase from scratch to be able to run very quickly and easily from scratch.
Um and if these builds ever fail because your codebase is rapidly changing. Uh we also have Devon be the first response there. And they're always immediately fixing these VM snapshots.

Um and by the way, these agents, you need to teach them how to test your codebase as well. But the benefit of using cloud coding agents is that they can self maintain their training loops. So that last section there on testing. Devin will write its own skills for how to test our codebase.

So the end result of this is literally people do not need to open their laptops anymore to test any code changes. In fact, several engineers at Cognition have already moved to using iPads for the development process.

scenes.alignment_note: The speaker walks through each panel of the slide: moving from AWS live services to isolated Docker Compose VMs, hourly VM snapshot rebuilds, and automated skill files (SKILL.md).

So you can do quite advanced setups if you really push the limits of your codebase.

spoken_segments.text: Um, and it actually on top of all of this, you know, you obviously want recursive self-improvement. I think people think about this from the model sense quite a lot.

But actually, if you think about it, every single line of code that's being written, every single PR that's being generated, every decision, if you have a cloud agent set up, that's all tracked across your entire codebase.
So there's no reason why you shouldn't also be able to run agents on top of that, do the data analysis and figure out, where are we wasting time, where are we wasting tokens?

And so we have a channel where Devin every day posts ideas about, hey, if we change our node setup, we can say shave like a minute off of our CI. If we change this lint script, we can like catch 20% more of these bugs before they ever hit AI code review.
Um, and this has actually been a huge unlock where you can just set up these systems and the agents will go and optimize your software factory for you.

scenes.alignment_note: The speaker points to the Analyzer node in the center node cluster and reads through the four specific factory optimization callout boxes on the right.

scenes.screen_title: We Give Agents Jobs, not Tasks
scenes.visual_summary: Title slide introducing a shift in engineering strategy: moving from prompting agents with small discrete tasks to giving them long-running, metric-driven autonomous jobs.
ocr_details: We Give Agents Jobs, not Tasks
scenes.structured_reconstruction: Section Title: We Give Agents Jobs, not Tasks

spoken_segments.text: Um, this has been really exciting. One of the things that I don't hear people talking about a lot, but I think it's really where things are going next is moving from the world where you're giving tasks to your agents to giving jobs to your agents.
And this is a bit of a paradigm shift. You you really have to start treating these things like coworkers. So what does giving a job to an agent look like?

scenes.alignment_note: Transition slide emphasizing the paradigm shift from task-level prompting to outcome-based agent jobs.

scenes.screen_title: From delegating tasks to delegating outcomes
scenes.visual_summary: Architecture diagram displaying the 4-stage job loop: 1) Human expresses desire ('Make our P99 endpoint latency faster'), 2) Devin defines goals & KPIs (840ms -> 500ms, 5,000 ACUs approved), 3) Devin scans codebase & creates 14 issues, 4) Devin continuously monitors & reports progress via Slack mobile alerts.
ocr_details: From delegating tasks to delegating outcomes
Walden: Make our P99 endpoint latency faster.
scenes.structured_reconstruction:
flowchart LR
    Stage1[Human: Express a desire
'Make our P99 endpoint latency faster'] --> Stage2[Devin defines goals & KPIs
From 840ms -> 500ms | 5,000 ACUs approved]
    Stage2 --> Stage3[Devin scans & creates tasks
14 issues: Batch order lookups, Add indexes, Alerts]
    Stage3 --> Stage4[Devin monitors & reports
Slack Mobile Alert: P99 down 65%]

spoken_segments.text: Imagine I care about backend performance. Really this is what the development flow the future should look like. You should send to your agent, hey, I want to improve P99 latency of my application.
Instead of you telling it what to do to do that, it should say, okay, P99 latency. Let me add the telemetry to figure out where our P99 latency is today.
Let me set up alerts so I can figure out where we need to be in the future.

Let me go break down every single task we need to do to be able to move this latency, let me create Datadog alerts, let me create weekly reports in Slack, and let me send you updates on your phone every day on here's where P99 latency is, and here's how much it's improved.
This is fundamentally the type of systems that we encourage all of our engineers to be building a cognition. We don't even we don't even want you to be prompting your agents most of the time.
We want you to just be giving your agent goals that they can work toward over long durations of time. And anything in your company that you think isn't measurable, find a way to measure it.

scenes.alignment_note: The speaker points across the 4 stages from left to right, referencing the initial latency prompt through to the automated Slack mobile report.

spoken_segments.text: So, a great example of this is inference latency. At cognition, we're lucky to be the first receivers of Nvidia's new class of Vero Reuben GPUs.
Kernels were not built for these GPUs or we received them. So we had to from scratch figure out how do we build our own inferrence stack on top of these this new hardware that's coming out.

And agents have allowed us to do this in a way that is much more efficient than before. So, we just tell it, hey, we care about the throughput or TPM of these GPUs. Go figure out how to push that to its limits.

And over the course of what is about I guess here like a week. Um the agent was able to go we we allocated a a permanent set of GPUs to work on. It was able to go find different strategies, test them.

Uh the strategies that it found worked best it would send to a human engineer for final approval. But basically there's eight or nine different things that were roughly discovered via just giving these agents these high-level goals and we were able to push uh the throughput on these new NVidia Rubin GPUs from what was worse than the new GB300s to what is now significantly better than the previous class of GB300 GPUs.

scenes.alignment_note: The speaker points to the benchmark curve rising above the GB300 (17,185) line up to 27,336 TPM and references the list of 8 changes engineered by Devin.

spoken_segments.text: Another example that I like to share with folks. We we are a fairly small engineering team. It means we do not have often times the bandwidth to fully staff things that we might want to do like our Android application.

But the other day, one of our engineers in our team Samuel. He had this brilliant idea. He said okay look, we have a team of people working on building a great iOS application. Can't we just use that as a blueprint for our Android application and tell Devon hey go maintain parity with from our iOS application to our Android application end to end.

But it wasn't just hey one Devon session to go do all this. He said setup permanent hooks against our codebase to monitor the iOS application. Uh you know, go listen to the Slack channels for user feedback about our applications, and then go recursively improve our application.
